item.title: Our Sense of Specialness
item.description:
Freudian Psychology

Our Sense of Specialness

Do we unconsciously reject mortality?

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • People may possess a sense of specialness—that we either are or should be exempt from death.
  • Freud believed that at the unconscious level, we do not believe in our own death.
  • This can affect the experience of mortality, such as receiving a terminal diagnosis.

A man who had served in the army once shared with me a joke about soldiers’ attitudes toward death. It went something like this:

A high-ranking officer turns to a close subordinate and says, “If the general is killed, I will assume his place. If I get injured, you will take mine.”

The quip captures the essence of the phenomenon that interests me here: our sense of specialness. By this, I do not mean a tendency to think we are gifted or possessed of a rare personality profile, or else that we differ from the rest of humanity in some other similar way. These latter tendencies exist, no doubt, but I don’t know how common they really are. At any rate, they are not what interests me here. What I wish to discuss is a sense of specialness that I believe to be exceedingly widespread: the sense that we either are or should be exempt from death. The high-ranking officer from the joke above speaks, to some extent, for all of us when he shows himself willing to imagine another’s death but not his own. He, and the rest of us, it seems, are not special even in thinking we are: Others think so too.

Freud, in an essay on death, suggests similarly that at the unconscious level, we do not believe in our own death but that we accept the mortality of other people, even those we love. Adults, in his view, restrain themselves from acknowledging that they think others — particularly loved ones — may die, but children may not. Writes Freud:

Children … are quite capable of giving expression to the thought of death in relation to the persons they love, as, for instance: Dear Mama, when unfortunately, you are dead, I shall do so and so.

To be clear, almost none of us believe consciously we are immortal. We know we are human, and that all humans die. Indeed, at one level, we take death to be one of the few things one can count on. Freud himself observes that fear of death regulates much of our behavior. But this fear remains somehow superficial. We often do not quite believe we are going to die. This is why people diagnosed with terminal illness not infrequently react with surprise and dismay.

Psychiatrist Irvin Yalom, in a discussion of the sense of specialness that interests me, puts the matter thus:

When an individual learns he or she has some serious illness — for example, cancer — the first reaction is generally some form of denial… once the individual really grasps, “My God, I'm really going to die,” and realizes that life will deal with him or her in the same harsh way as it deals with others, he or she feels lost and, in some odd way, betrayed.1

Why should we feel betrayed to learn the approximate date of what always knew was coming?

And are we flawed for assuming, however unconsciously and unreflectively, that we won’t, in the final analysis, die? These are the questions that interest me here.

Source: T. Royce Xan/Pexels

Is Specialness a Defense?

Yalom, in the chapter I quoted from, suggests that the implicit expectation we won’t die is self-protective: what it protects us from is fear of death. There is certainly truth to the hypothesis. It is probably healthy not to obsess over that which is inevitable. There is something adaptive and healthy about living as though we didn’t know. The hiddenness, the felt unreality of our own mortality may enable us to live good lives in much the way divine hiddenness is said by the philosopher Kant to enable moral life: Kant suggests that if God’s presence were constantly salient, we would never act for moral reasons but only out of fear of punishment. We can say, similarly, that if the thought of our own death fully “sunk in,” we’d be unable to enjoy life or to make progress toward our goals.

Yet, one can argue, alternatively, that it would be good to accept our own mortality early on so that we don’t spend years procrastinating and expending time and energy on trivial worries and pursuits. In addition, false beliefs protect only before the truth is discovered. If we did not have a propensity to be lulled into a false sense of inviolability, we would never be forced to feel “slighted” by the hand of fortune and “betrayed” in the Yalom speaks of in the passage I quoted.

Freud, in the essay on death I quoted from, makes a slightly different proposal. Having argued that “Our unconscious … does not believe in its own death” and “acts as though it were immortal,” he proceeds to observe that we cannot imagine our own death. To imagine one’s own funeral or the state of the world after one’s death is to imagine, in some way, surviving.

This hypothesis comes closer to my own view, to which I now turn.

Our Point of View

The most natural way to see the world is from one’s own point of view. Other people are neighbors or strangers, friends or foes in relation to us. The time and place where I live seem to me more real than any other in history. Indeed, we can imagine that we have hallucinated the rest of the world. The supposition, contrariwise, that it is we who are the unreal ones, that we are someone else’s hallucination, verges on incoherence. Our perspective on the world is our default perspective. From it, however, we are the “center” of the world.

It is possible, of course, to adopt a different viewpoint — someone else’s or that of a spectator. However, doing so requires work and imagination and success is at best partial. It is not simply that we cannot imagine our own death because there is nothing there for us to imagine, as Freud argued, but that a world without us in it seems strange and alien: it is a disorganized flux. There are multiple people in it, with their own points of view, but no one’s perspective is privileged in the way ours is for us, since none is a perspective we know or can know intimately: each is a product of another’s mind. A world without us is, thus, a world without an anchoring consciousness; one in which the center does not hold.

Philosopher Sarah Buss suggests that our own sense of specialness, the tendency to ask "Why me?" if we get diagnosed with cancer, for instance, as if we, unlike other people, are not supposed to die, is in some way morally shameful because it betrays unacceptable privileging of ourselves. If the foregoing considerations are right, that sense has a source more primordial than morality: it stems from the fact that our default perspective on the world involves our own existence. It does not involve anyone else's existence.

This sense of specialness may create a moral problem only if it ceases to be a deeply ingrained disposition and becomes conviction: if from the fact it is easier to imagine the death of others we infer that others are more worthy of dying.

I don’t think many hold that view. Indeed, as Buss herself notes, there is the reverse phenomenon of survivor’s guilt: of asking why it is I who didn't die.

item.title: The Non-Physical Trait Most Desired in a Romantic Partner
item.description:
Relationships

The Non-Physical Trait Most Desired in a Romantic Partner

When seeking love, the most attractive trait is not appearance.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling known and knowing your partner are separate predictors of relationship satisfaction.
  • In crafting dating profiles, people strongly express a desire to be known.
  • Feeling known leads to perception of good relational support.

Anyone looking for love likely has an idea of what they would ideally desire in a partner. And appearance is only one component. One of the most desirable traits in a prospective partner is authentic interest. Everyone wants to find someone who is uniquely fascinated with them, and genuinely interested in their hopes, dreams, and feelings. This is how relationships form among people from all types of different demographics and backgrounds, bound together by mutual interest, love, and respect. How do these people find each other?

Getting to Know You—and Getting to Be Known

Everyone can relate to meeting someone, personally or professionally, who makes a great impression through expressing selfless, genuine interest. We enjoy spending time with such individuals at social events or meetings even though we are doing most of the talking, because an authentically receptive audience is a breath of fresh air in an era of selfies and social media updates. When we meet someone who is authentically interested in us, we remember them. Fondly. Research explains how this works.

Juliana Schroeder and Ayelet Fishbach (2024) explored the attraction of feeling known by a partner in a piece entitled “Feeling Known Predicts Relationship Satisfaction.”[i] They start by recognizing that two forms of subjective relationship knowledge, believing you are known and knowing your partner, are separate predictors of relationship satisfaction. Regarding which is more important for relational wellbeing, they found through performing multiple studies involving friends, family, and romantic partners, that feeling known by a partner is a greater predictor of relationship satisfaction than believing one knows their partner.

The Attraction of Authentic Attention

With respect to dating, Schroeder and Fishbach found that in crafting dating profiles designed to attract potential paramours, individuals more strongly expressed their desire to be known than to get to know potential partners. Yet ironically, profile readers were more attracted to others who professed interest in getting to know them. Accordingly, Schroeder and Fishbach note that attracting a relationship partner may require expressing a desire to get to know them rather than solely asking them to get to know you.

Schroeder and Fishbach also recognize the implications their research has on considering what is really important when seeking a relationship partner. They recognize scholarship indicating how men prefer attractive women and women prefer rich men (citing e.g., Buss & Schmitt, 2019), as well as research highlighting traits with worldwide appeal such as compassion and humor (citing Joel et al., 2017). Yet their results suggest online daters are looking for more, seeking partners who desire to know them rather than partners who want to be known. They note that consequently, rather than focusing on one attractive trait or set of traits, it is the motivational mindset of interest in being known that drives the search for the perfect partner. In this respect, they recognize their findings are more consistent with prior research considering other motivational factors impacting decisions to start relationships, such as a fear of being single (citing Spielmann et al., 2013).

Schroeder and Fishbach also recognize that the fact that feeling known in a relationship is more important to relationship satisfaction than feeling like one knows their partner indicates that feeling known leads to feeling supported. Accordingly, if enjoying a relationship depends more on perceiving good support than providing it, feeling known will be more highly linked with relationship satisfaction than believing they know their partner.

Authentic Interest Prompts Permanence

Authentic desire to know your partner is perceivable. Someone can only pretend to be interested for so long before people see through the false flattery or inauthentic attention. Genuine concern and compassion for others is transparent and builds trust. When seeking relational permanence, better to select a prospective partner who you authentically want to get to know, and who conversely, is genuinely interested in you.

item.title: Should You Do '180-Dating' After a Breakup?
item.description:
Mating

Should You Do '180-Dating' After a Breakup?

Trying something new can open up your dating horizons.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • The 180-dating trend on social media is about going for the "opposite" of your type.
  • A breakup can be a good opportunity to see how you might want to change your dating preferences.
  • The degree to which 180-dating works depends on how earnestly you want to learn about yourself and others.
Source: Rawpixel/Shutterstock

So you have been recovering from a breakup and are ready to circle back to the dating market. Will you be seeking more of the same as your ex? Or is it time to follow this whole "180-dating" trend on social media and the internet—namely, going for someone who is the opposite? Well, whether you make such a 180-degree turn does depend on the degree to which you truly know yourself and have already tried different things.

A Breakup Is a Good Opportunity to Reassess Your Dating Preferences

A breakup is sort of like the end of a sports season when a team didn't win the championship and typically reassesses its entire strategy, approach, and personnel and determines what changes are needed for the next season. That's because finishing anywhere but on top is usually a sign that something wasn't completely right.

Similarly, breakups don't typically result from you and your ex fitting just too darn well with each other. Instead, some significant mismatch was there. Or maybe even multiple red-flag-level mismatches that you simply didn't notice while you were too busy listening to your body, your fear of being single, or whatever you shouldn't have been listening to so much. Therefore, a breakup can be a good "check engine light" opportunity to take stock of not just your latest ex but also your dating history overall and determine whether they truly fit with your personality, goals, and values.

Sure, your latest ex could have been like a visit to an inebriated barber or hairstylist—a one-time mistake. However, if your ex fell into "your type"—meaning the same type of person that you've kept dating repeatedly—then this latest breakup could be the right time to change your dating trajectory up a bit—or a lot. You know the saying, "Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results." Well, the same old, same old, may not be the sane old, sane old if "you too" still haven't yet found what you are looking for.

How 180-Dating Can Help

The 180-dating approach could force change—disrupt any tendency to simply stick with what you know. Picture your dating tendencies as a tide that's been pushing you in the wrong direction—away from the land that you want to reach. The next step then could be swimming directly against the tide.

This can be especially useful if you haven't yet experienced much diversity in your dating. Maybe your "checklist" has been automatically ruling out people based on characteristics and qualities that in the end won't really matter that much. You never know what someone or something might actually be like until you actually try it—with the possible exception of wearing sweater vests. Therefore, 180-dating can open you up to new possibilities.

article continues after advertisement

A 180 could also help you put a big "X" on memories of and longing for your ex. Seeing someone different could help you focus on different things and essentially move on from your prior relationship. The contrast can give you better perspective on what you do and do not ultimately want, as well.

Determine How You Want To Apply 180-Dating

Of course, what exactly you end up doing a 180 on does matter. A change-up on very superficial characteristics like race, height, and other appearance things can make total sense and help you realize how little they matter. These certainly are trivial compared to more core things like values, goals, and personality that are more likely to determine the fate of a relationship.

Doing a 180 on more core things, though, can be a different story. You may have already figured out certain super important non-negotiables that may be best left in place and not 180'd. For example, say having a partner that you can trust is something of core importance to you. Obviously, it may not be worthwhile to do a 180 on fidelity then and go for someone who would cheat on you at the drop of a hat.

That being said, going 180 on different characteristics can help you figure out what characteristics are actually core and matter to you. You might find that you've been mistaken about certain characteristics. In fact, you could have been opting for a certain type of person largely because you thought that such a type would be more likely to have some underlying characteristic that you truly want.

Let's take an age-old example. A stereotype is that people of the same age group have more in common with each other. Another stereotype is that those older are more stable and mature. A third stereotype is that those younger are more flexible and curious.

But none of these may be the case for different individuals. An older person can be just as immature as a much younger person. At the same time, lots of younger people can be inflexible with little curiosity. You may find that you have much more in common with a younger or older person because what you are truly interested in is a certain level of maturity, flexibility, or curiosity.

article continues after advertisement

Figure Out What 180-Dating Means

Of course, doing a 180 isn't an exact science involving a protractor or some kind of app that can precisely measure angles. Sure, some things have clear exact opposites. Many other things, though, don't. So, be careful about making it seem like something—like a certain background, upbringing, or interest—is the exact opposite of another.

Instead, maybe view 180-dating as an opportunity to get more of a 360-degree view of what is out there and yourself. In the end, the degree to which 180-dating works depends on the degree to which you earnestly want to learn about yourself and other people. If you are simply doing this as a gimmick, then you could end up spiraling and never figure out the true right fit for you.

item.title: What Imposter Syndrome Has Been Trying to Tell You All Along
item.description:
Imposter Syndrome

What Imposter Syndrome Has Been Trying to Tell You All Along

Why "liminal tension" is the growth signal your mind keeps trying to send.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Imposter syndrome is the belief you don't belong in the room.
  • Most people interpret this tension as a sign to back off and avoid entering the room.
  • By learning to see this tension as a sign to lean in and grow, you can unlock new opportunities.

No matter how much expertise, ambition, or discipline you have, imposter syndrome can hold you back from fully stepping into what you know you’re capable of.

A lot of the work I do as a psychologist-turned-executive coach is helping founders, leaders, and creators remove the psychological bottlenecks costing them business growth, and imposter syndrome is one of the most common psychological bottlenecks I see.

Imposter syndrome, fundamentally, is the belief that you don’t belong in the room—whatever that room is (physical, virtual, or conceptual). So if you attempt to enter that room, you feel a cognitive resistance—a tension that most people interpret as a sign to back off.

But what if it isn't a sign to back off?

Conceptualizing it as “imposter syndrome” misdiagnoses what you’re going through. Instead, I like to use the term liminal tension, and here’s why.

The Problem with Imposter Syndrome

When you mentally label the tension you feel as imposter syndrome, it can make you think you’re a fraud who doesn’t belong.

So anytime you start to enter a room and feel that tension, you pull back and tell yourself you need to wait until you feel “ready” or “prepared” before you try to enter the room again. “Then,” you tell yourself, “I’ll belong in the room.” Because everyone else in that room clearly deserves to be there because they have more expertise, more success, or are somehow superior to you in some way.

This is why labeling it as imposter syndrome holds you back. You have integrity, so you obviously don’t want people to think you’re a fraud, and you definitely don’t want to feel like a fraud internally.

So you wait until that magical day when you won’t feel like a fraud before you enter those bigger, better, scarier rooms.

But that day never comes, so you spend your entire life pulling back every time you’re on the precipice of a new room.

That “new room” can be a physical one like speaking at a conference, a conceptual one like publishing a book that could sit on the same shelf as your favorite authors, or even an identity one like shifting from seeing yourself as a solopreneur of a tiny company to a CEO of a company you’ve scaled into a “real” business.

Instead, you can learn to see that exact same tension as a good sign—a sign to lean in instead of pull back. If you re-label it as liminal tension.

According to Merriam-Webster, "liminal" comes from the Latin limen, which means "threshold". It describes being in an intermediate state, phase, or condition.

So a liminal space is the area between two things. It’s like a hallway between two rooms. While you’re in the hallway, you’re on your way from one room to the other, but you’re not in either. And right as you’re about to enter the room the hallway leads to, you have to cross the threshold to that new room.

article continues after advertisement

It’s at this threshold that we feel maximum tension because it’s the final step before we actually enter the new room—the room we’ve maybe never been in before. And since we’ve never been in this room before, it’s easy to doubt ourselves into believing we don’t belong in the room.

Identity Ambiguity

When you try to take action that doesn’t align with your identity, you experience cognitive dissonance—which feels like mental static or anxiety because there’s a discrepancy between your self-belief and behavior. Which means if you want to take action to enter the room, you have to believe you belong in the room in the first place. Otherwise, you’ll self-sabotage (aka, change your behavior) to preserve the belief that you don’t belong in the room.

Put another way, identity is the foundation of aligned action. If you don’t believe you’re worthy of being in the room, you won’t take action to enter the room.

I see this all the time in my work with founders. Highly ambitious, accomplished, and disciplined people memorizing all the productivity “hacks” and trying to take action over and over, but always somehow sabotaging their success at the last minute. Because their identity is holding them back.

It’s not woo-woo to say you have to believe in yourself. It’s human psychology. Our behaviors are downstream of our beliefs. Everything we do, every action we take, and every thought we have is rooted in our beliefs (about ourselves and the world around us). We’re driven to reinforce our own schema of the world and ourselves, meaning we take actions that align with what we believe is true, possible, and deserved.

So if you believe you belong in the room, you’ll take the action of crossing the threshold. If you believe you don’t belong in the room, you’ll take the action to avoid crossing the threshold.

But if you learn to label that feeling as liminal tension, a sign you’re challenging yourself to grow, it’s much easier to cross that threshold. Because you’re not expecting perfection before you cross it, you’re pursuing growth by crossing it.

When I decided to become a public speaker and lead workshops and presentations for conferences, there was obviously a point where I’d never done it before and had to cross the threshold into leading my first one. I could’ve easily told myself I didn’t belong in the room—or “Who am I to call myself a public speaker?” But instead I reframed it as “Stepping into this opportunity, this room, will help me grow into the person I know I’m capable of becoming.” I had to lean into the liminal tension that came up as I crossed the threshold from being not-a-speaker to being a speaker.

That liminal tension will always be there when you attempt to enter a new room because it represents the threshold of a new identity, a new skillset, a new life. What you’re feeling is the tension of growth, of evolution, of actualizing your potential.

Seeing it as liminal tension helps you reframe the initial belief of “This is a room I don’t belong in” into “This is a room where I’ll grow in.” And that allows you to take the aligned action of leaning in instead of pulling back to stay in your comfort zone.

article continues after advertisement

How to Embrace Liminal Tension

“The fastest way to change your life is to force yourself to level up by placing yourself in an environment where you feel like you don’t belong.” — Jay Yang, author of You Can Just Do Things

Take a second and reflect.

There’s a room right now that you’ve been at the threshold of entering for a while now, but keep pulling back because you label that discomfort as imposter syndrome. You’re not a fraud. You’re on the precipice of growth. But the longer you delay entering that room, the longer you delay your growth. And you have too much potential to keep doing that.

What if instead, you chose to see that tension as a sign of growth and decided to lean into it?

What if you told yourself, “This tension is supposed to be here. I’m supposed to feel this because it means I’m growing and pushing myself.” How would that change how you act right now?

Pull out a notecard and write down this reminder:

The growth you seek is in the room you’re avoiding.

Now that you've reframed imposter syndrome as liminal tension, what tension will you lean into? What evolution will you finally give yourself permission to embrace? What new identity will you step into?

item.title: Do We Live in an Unjust World?
item.description:
Wisdom

Do We Live in an Unjust World?

Prospering is not the same as flourishing.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Injustice may bring wealth and power, but these are not the same as flourishing.
  • The tyrant appears supremely free but is enslaved by fear and appetite.
  • Only the just life can lead to freedom and fulfillment.
The sword of Damocles: the most unjust person may also be the least free.
Source: AI-generated.

We have to recognise that we do live in an unjust world—a stupidly unjust world. Bad people often prosper, while goodness and virtue carry no guarantee of wealth, fame, power, or even security.

But prospering is not the same as flourishing. Injustice can only secure the external goods of life. Though injustice can make us wealthy and powerful, it cannot make us wise, tranquil, or contented.

The tyrant is the perfect test case of what I’m saying. The tyrant, almost by definition, is the most unjust person, seemingly enjoying the greatest possible success. Of course, not every unjust person is a tyrant, but the tyrant reveals, in its most extreme form, what injustice does to the person who practises it.

Seneca and Nero

The Stoic philosopher Seneca, who lived in the first century CE, once wrote a long letter to the tyrannical Roman emperor, Nero. In this letter, he warns Nero that the most powerful person in a tyranny may also be the least free. We don’t know whether he actually sent the letter, but a large part of it has come down to us. It’s called On Clemency. Clemency, says Seneca, is the trait that most distinguishes a king from a tyrant—and by winning admiration and loyalty, helps to keep the king safe and free. The tyrant, on the other hand, becomes the prisoner of his own power: he is hated because he is feared, and must make himself feared because he is hated. It’s a vicious cycle. In the end, he cannot travel freely or trust even his closest advisors. He cannot sleep soundly in his bed or take his meals without fearing that someone might have poisoned his food.

Few tyrants die in their own bed, and so it proved also with Nero, who ended his own life to evade capture. He did not even have the courage to wield the dagger: his freedman had to help him drive it into his throat. His final, deluded words were: Qualis artifex pereo—‘What an artist dies in me!’ Perhaps his last thought was of Seneca.

Plato’s Tyrant

If Seneca showed us the tyrant’s political prison, Plato showed us his psychological prison, the prison inside him. The tyrant’s soul is ruled by lawless appetites which he can neither control nor satisfy. Thus, the man who appears supremely free is in fact a slave to his own deranged psychology. He has conquered everyone except himself.

article continues after advertisement

In Plato’s Republic, Socrates calculates, by some fanciful Platonic mathematics, that the true king is precisely 729 times happier than the tyrant!

How to Guard Against Tyrants

But philosophy cannot content itself with pointing out that the tyrant is miserable. The fate and suffering of the tyrant hardly make up for all his injustices—for all the injustices that he imposes upon others on his way up and then on his way down. That’s why we need to have much stronger safeguards against tyrants.

To guard against the rise of a tyrant, here are three things that we could do. First, we need to make sure that a career in politics remains desirable to decent people—or end up being governed only by power-hungry people. Second, we need to strengthen education so that every citizen can recognise the tyrant’s old bag of tricks. And third, we need to bolster constitutions and institutions so that they are able to arrest the rise of a would-be tyrant, no matter how insistent or popular they may be. We have put astronauts into space, invented nuclear reactors and artificial intelligence—so this, surely, is not beyond us.

Prospering vs Flourishing

So, yes, we live in an unjust world—a stupidly unjust world. Bad people prosper, while innocent people suffer. But prospering is not the same as flourishing. Only a life well lived can lead to the true goods of life: wisdom, freedom, tranquillity, contentedness. These are all internal goods which external goods may support, but can never guarantee.

But to lead a just life is not merely a winning strategy. It is also a refusal to become a part of the problem.

item.title: New Year, New Teachers
item.description:
Resilience

New Year, New Teachers

Your child's new teacher might not be a great fit for them, but that's okay.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Not every teacher is going to be a perfect fit for your child, but it might work out well in the end.
  • Don't let your children hear you talk negatively about their teachers.
  • A little classroom adversity can be a good thing.

As a parent myself, I understand that it is desirable for children to have positive experiences with teachers who nurture their strengths and assist them in compensating for their weaknesses. However, teachers are individuals with their own personalities. There is no way for every teacher to be a great fit for every student. Just as students have different learning styles, teachers have different teaching styles, and there will be times when a teacher-student match is not perfect. Maybe the teacher's personality is strict and the child prefers nurturance, or maybe the teacher is a stickler for detail, and the child feels the grading is unfair. This is not only true for a child's experience throughout school, but it will be true for their experience throughout life. A supervisor's managerial style will not always be to the preference of all their employees.

Throughout my posts in this column, I have continually discussed how important it is for children and teens to have the opportunity to practice life skills throughout their childhood. Well, having a teacher who is not a perfect fit is a great opportunity to practice tolerance, patience, and empathy for individual differences. Working a little bit harder to make it work is actually a good thing.

Stay Positive about the Teacher(s)

Who can answer this question?
Source: Max Fisher / Pexels

When parents are vocal about their disapproval of their child's teachers, it gives their child an excuse to avoid taking responsibility. The child may begin to blame the teacher's grading policies, bias against them, or poor teaching skills as the reason not to work hard in class. So instead of getting a B (when maybe they deserved an A, which might be unfair), they get a C, lunch detentions, and/or feel angry throughout the year. Furthermore, since it is easier to blame someone else than take responsibility, this can quickly develop into a pattern. Children have a choice about how they deal with adversity, and as a parent, you can help them navigate these difficult situations by promoting social skills and problem-solving.

Whether a situation is truly unfair or not, parents should never put their child in the victim role. Once a child feels they are the victim, they might stop taking responsibility and feel that all problems are the fault of someone else. On the other hand, if parents guide their children in coping with the situation, then they get practice dealing with difficult interpersonal situations. Something positive from something negative.

Before your child even reaches high school, they will probably have at least 20 different teachers. Therefore, chances are likely to have a few teachers who aren't a great match for their learning style or personality. Under no circumstances should children hear parents complain about a teacher. As soon as a child thinks you don't like a teacher, they have no choice but to align with you as the parent. This results in reduced motivation and effort in the classroom and a missed chance to practice overcoming challenges. Make this year one of the best for your child, even if their teacher isn’t a perfect fit.

item.title: 3 Reasons Some People Are Ashamed to Admit They Use AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

3 Reasons Some People Are Ashamed to Admit They Use AI

How AI use threatens identity, authenticity, and ups the fear of being judged.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Some people worry that AI makes their accomplishments feel less authentic.
  • AI use can threaten people's identities, but it does not have to.
  • People may fear being plied up on by others and shamed for using AI.

This past week, a counseling client of mine who works for a company on the cusp of high-level breakthrough technology endeavors told me, in the strict confidence of my office, that she and her team use AI. So what, maybe you say? Well, please hear that just three months ago she said she would never use AI because, as a "coding purist", she eschewed it.

This woman is just one of many examples where I keep hearing people say something like, “I don’t use AI" or that they hate AI—but they use it. When it comes to writing with AI versus using it for coding, someone else told me just last week that a book they wrote was “100 percent human.” They then told me they were lying because they felt ashamed to admit they used AI to help them brainstorm.

The Cautions for AI Make Sense, But the Shame Doesn't

By now, we have all heard the legitimate concerns that AI can be confidently wrong (and as it gets smarter, that will become less and less the case), or that it can make cheating and intellectual laziness easier. And then there are cognitive offloading concerns. That's a fancy way of saying that when we hand stuff over to AI, we aren't using our intellectual muscles and are dumbing ourselves down.

But going back to my client I mentioned at the beginning, something else is happening. For some people, admitting they use AI is becoming a little (and in some cases a lot) embarrassing—or worse, shaming. Why is that? Well, here are the three reasons I see at play in our new culture of AI self-shaming and the fear of being AI-shamed by others.

1. We Worry That AI Makes Our Accomplishments Feel Less Authentic

I have heard many conversations about AI that rest on an increasingly absurd assumption: If a machine helped, the accomplishment somehow counts less. Yet we’ve always accepted help with our thinking, haven't we? Way back, the ancient philosophers used scribes, as discussed in the post, LLMs: The Dynamic Scribes of Our Age, by fellow Psychology Today blogger John Nosta. His core point is that writers have editors, including the scribes who served the great philosophers; students have teachers; and professionals consult colleagues. In short, since the dawn of time, someone can challenge an idea or point out something we missed without taking ownership of what we ultimately decide. So, while AI certainly raises new questions, using this tool collaboratively and surrendering your thinking to it are not necessarily the same thing.

2. AI Threatens The Identities That We Value

If I take pride in being a good writer, what does it mean that a machine can produce a competent (or often excellent) paragraph in seconds? I keep coming back to the legend of John Henry, the steel-driving man who raced a steam-powered drill. John Henry wins, but in the legend, the effort costs him his life. The story has lasted because it captures something deeply human. We want to know that the machine hasn’t made us unnecessary, yet AI may be stirring that same anxiety.

This reminds me of something I write about in my book When Overthinking Overtakes Your Child. Overthinking can pull us toward either-or conclusions because certainty feels more comfortable than ambiguity. Something is right or wrong, safe or dangerous. As adults, we do this too, and with AI, it can become similarly polarized as human or artificial, authentic or fake, thinking for yourself or letting a machine think for you.

3. We Fear Being the Person Everyone Piles On

Think about a fumble on a football field. Once the pile starts forming, players dive in from everywhere. Some have almost no chance of recovering the ball, but they still jump into the scrum and may even throw an elbow while they’re there. Sometimes conversations about AI can feel a little like that. With criticizing AI use becoming socially acceptable, it's easy to pile on.

Fear of shame makes people less willing to admit things, including AI use. At its worst, it can even smell like a feared ideological purity test: Did you use AI? How much? Did it write that sentence? Is this really yours? These questions can create maddening overthinking loops and start to matter more than the quality of your own thinking itself.

Final Thoughts

For sure, there are situations where AI shouldn't be used, and others where disclosure matters. But perhaps we should spend less time asking whether someone used AI and more time asking what they did with it. Or, dare I push the envelope here, but what if they used AI and it improved their output? Or do we just want to be John Henrys, destroy ourselves, and miss out on feeling good about using the amazing gifts AI offers us?
